Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 67
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Doctor
  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 54

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time
  Threat: Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
  Memory: Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it, No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself

Vignette:
Dr. Eduardo Vasquez still remembers the summer his son Mateo turned seven—not as a season of birthday parties and baseball games, but as a blur of hospital corridors, beeping monitors, and the acrid smell of antiseptic. A previously healthy boy, suddenly febrile and limp, diagnosed with bacterial meningitis within hours of arrival at the emergency department where Eduardo himself had worked for two decades. As a physician, he knew the statistics, knew the protocols, knew that every second mattered. But as a father, standing beside the gurney while a resident started the IV, he felt something crack open inside him. The memory of those seventy-two hours never cohered into a story he could tell himself. When he tries now to recall the sequence of events—the lumbar puncture, the frantic phone calls to specialists, the moment the attending physician finally said the steroids were working—the details slip away like water through his fingers. He knows what happened, but the words won't come. The picture is incomplete: isolated images of Mateo’s face, pale against the pillow, and the sound of his own voice, hoarse from repeating the same question to every nurse who passed. He cannot piece it together, not even for himself, not even in the dark of his own bedroom at night.

In the years that followed, Eduardo learned to keep his mind occupied. He threw himself into shifts at the hospital, volunteering for the most complex cases, staying late to read journals, attending every continuing education seminar he could find. At home, he filled the silence with podcasts, news radio, the television left on in the background. If a thought about Mateo’s illness surfaced—a memory of the way the light had slanted through the blinds in the ICU, the particular pitch of the cardiac monitor alarm—he pushed it away, hard and fast. He tried hard not to think about the trauma, and for long stretches, he succeeded. But the effort itself was exhausting, and he began to notice that he was always watching, always waiting—scanning the faces of patients for signs of sepsis, checking his own pulse at odd moments, listening for the catch in Mateo’s voice when he called from college. The hypervigilance followed him everywhere. At work, he flinched when a code was called overhead; at the grocery store, the sight of a child with a feverish flush sent a jolt of adrenaline through his chest.

Strong negative feelings ambushed him without warning. Guilt, mostly—that he hadn’t caught the symptoms sooner, that he hadn’t demanded the attending move faster, that he had ever allowed himself to feel relief when the crisis passed. Sometimes it was anger, aimless and hot, directed at no one in particular. And then there were the flashbacks. They came without trigger, or so it seemed: suddenly, in the middle of a consult, he would be back in that room, the fluorescent lights humming, the smell of saline, the weight of Mateo’s hand in his. He would feel his heart race, his palms sweat, and for a terrifying moment the present would dissolve. He had learned to excuse himself, to find a supply closet or a bathroom stall, to breathe until the world returned.

His avoidance had consequences. He stopped attending family gatherings where children might be sick; he declined invitations to colleagues’ homes, afraid that a child’s cough would undo him. His relationships narrowed. He remained single, a fact he told himself was a preference for independence, but in truth he could not imagine letting anyone close enough to have that kind of power over him again. At work, his meticulousness became a kind of armor: he double-checked every lab result, ordered extra tests, kept his patients longer in the ward than necessary. He was considered a thorough doctor, but his colleagues noticed he never spoke about his own life, never joined them for lunch, always seemed to be in a hurry to return to his rounds.

At sixty-seven, Eduardo had been retired for two years, and the structure that once held his avoidance together had crumbled. With no shifts to fill, no seminars to attend, the silence of his apartment pressed in on him. He found himself pacing the rooms, turning on every light, checking his phone for messages from Mateo—who was now a healthy thirty-four-year-old lawyer living in another state. The mental distraction had lost its power. He could no longer outrun the fragments of memory. An article in the newspaper about childhood illness sent him spiraling; a sudden sound of a siren outside his window left him trembling. His sleep was poor, his appetite gone.

What finally brought him to a therapist’s office was not an insight about PTSD, but a phone call from Mateo, who had noticed that his father never asked about his health anymore, never visited, never seemed to want to hear about his life. “You check out every time I mention the word hospital, Dad,” Mateo said, not accusing, just stating a fact. Eduardo could not deny it. He was terrified of what he might feel if he let himself remember fully, of the guilt that might drown him if he sat with the story. But he was also terrified of losing the last real connection he had. So he made the appointment. He sat in the waiting room, his hands folded, his jaw tight, not knowing how to begin—but knowing, for the first time, that he could not keep his mind occupied forever.
